chapter: Chicago repertoire, bands and the end of the big-band era
title: Gene Ammons, Billy Eckstine's band and the Chicago nucleus of Dizzy's band
summary: They discuss Jug's path from Kolax to Eckstine and Red Top, and how Diz drew on Hines, Eckstine and Kolax alumni.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: . . . with King Kolax and then with – to Billy Eckstine, because then he cut Red Top, and Jug never looked back.
When Gene Ammons was with Eckstine, Parker had already left.
So who was playing alto then at the time, with . . . ?
Sonny Stitt came in – he replaced Parker?
I think so. I’d have to read the book on that. But I’m almost certain that he did. Because he had all the cats: Dexter.
Yeah, I know almost everybody passed through his band.
Yeah, everybody went, because he was . . .
That’s where Diz got his band, was from Billy Eckstine’s band.
A lot of those guys were in Earl Hines’s band before that, right? A couple of them.
A couple of them, yeah. I think so.
I know Bird and Diz were.

And also I think that great trumpet player that ended up playing with my brother George. He was on Gene Ammons’s Red Top. Gail Brockman. All these cats had big names. Diz just – when he started that greatest band of the century, he more or less got them from Earl Hines and Billy Eckstine and King Kolax. That was the nucleus. Chicago at that time had a big, big name. The cats were all here. New York was – it was all right if you wanted to go there, but . . .
